[{:db/id 17592186092234 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-79a5f235-c3e4-525b-8b8a-0996cfbfc3bb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092233 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-111ba920-c11a-5d82-a4be-8a7616b01f46" "question-301cb6c3-bb47-52a5-b9af-9305c0ba1695"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092235 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3beff671-5436-54ac-a3ba-4902dc435008"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092687 :question/problem "If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =5.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ -4 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-10{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & -10 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-5}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186090322 :answer-field/correct 17592186090324 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287675 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =1.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=6,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{6}{-2}=-3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186357565 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =8.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 6 & 7\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 \\ 6 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-12{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 6 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-12 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-12{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=-12,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -12\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-12}{-2}=6.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-79a5f235-c3e4-525b-8b8a-0996cfbfc3bb" :question/id #uuid "79a5f235-c3e4-525b-8b8a-0996cfbfc3bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-107107" :question/problem "If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =3.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{-1}{3}=-\frac{1}{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dd938821-c74e-5b26-90b9-683b5bbf18c0"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-301cb6c3-bb47-52a5-b9af-9305c0ba1695" :question/id #uuid "301cb6c3-bb47-52a5-b9af-9305c0ba1695" :question/math-academy-id "q-18081" :question/problem "Find an eigenvector  of $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ -10 & -6\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\ -12 & 25\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -12 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\ -12{x}_{1}+18{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 & 0 \\ -12 & 18 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For $\lambda =29,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\ -12 & 25\end{aligned}]-29[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-18{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\ -12{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 & 0 \\ -12 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186244043 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

:question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-1.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-111ba920-c11a-5d82-a4be-8a7616b01f46" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3a06f774-759e-5d50-b56f-887b8f0a8b18" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 20 & 13\end{aligned}]$,
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$"] ["question-3beff671-5436-54ac-a3ba-4902dc435008" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 20 & 13\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 20 & 15\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}+15{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 20 & 15 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For $\lambda =17,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 20 & 13\end{aligned}]-17[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-15 & 3 \\ 20 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-15{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-15 & 3 & 0 \\ 20 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-15 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-3beff671-5436-54ac-a3ba-4902dc435008" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-99f559f8-f0c3-5b01-8f1d-d740f6f545ba" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation \n\n$$\n(A-\\lambda I)\\text{x}=0.\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. \n\n- For $\\lambda =7,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =[\\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\\\ -12 & 25\\end{aligned}]-7[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\\\ -12 & 18\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have a system of linear equations \n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\\\ -12{x}_{1}+18{x}_{2}=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwith the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}M & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & -6 & 0 \\\\ -12 & 18 & 0\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}4 & -6 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. \nFrom the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=\\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{aligned}],\\,{x}_{2}\\in R.\n$$\n\nSetting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector \n${v}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}].$\n\n- For $\\lambda =29,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =[\\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\\\ -12 & 25\\end{aligned}]-29[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 \\\\ -12 & -4\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have a system of linear equations \n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}-18{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\\\ -12{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwith the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}M & =[\\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 & 0 \\\\ -12 & -4 & 0\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}-18 & -6 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. \nFrom the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{aligned}],\\,{x}_{2}\\in R.\n$$\n\nSetting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector \n${v}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$\n\nTherefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}],[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186244113 :question/id #uuid \n\n- For $\\lambda =-2,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & -12 \\\\ 1 & -5\\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & -12 \\\\ 1 & -3\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have a system of linear equations \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}-12{x}_{2}=0 \\\\ {x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwith the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}M & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & -12 & 0 \\\\ 1 & -3 & 0\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\\frac{1}{4}){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}4 & -12 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. \nFrom the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{aligned}],\\,{x}_{2}\\in R.\n$$\n\nSetting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector \n${v}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$\n\n- For $\\lambda =-1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & -12 \\\\ 1 & -5\\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & -12 \\\\ 1 & -4\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have a system of linear equations \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-12{x}_{2}=0 \\\\ {x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwith the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}M & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & -12 & 0 \\\\ 1 & -4 & 0\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}3 & -12 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. \nFrom the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{aligned}],\\,{x}_{2}\\in R.\n$$\n\nSetting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector \n${v}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$\n\nTherefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ ![](images/30/30880937eed54b00cb0ebe13bd2a46e2634e4193343b1db552b30836ed1e055b.svg) Given that $\\lambda=3$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ how can we find an eigenvector that corresponds to this eigenvalue?\n\nRecall that a non-zero vector $\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with corresponding eigenvalue $\\lambda$ if \n\n$$\nA{\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}}={\\color{red}\\lambda}{\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}}.\n$$\n\nWe can rewrite this equation, substituting ${\\color{red}{\\lambda = 3}},$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Av & =3v \\\\ Av-3v & =0 \\\\ Av-3Iv & =0 \\\\ (A-3I)v & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, to find an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to $\\lambda = {\\color{red}3},$ we need to find a non-zero solution of the equation \n\n$$\n(A- {\\color{red}3} I){\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}} = \\mathbf{0}.\n$$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}]-3[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-1 & 6 \\\\ 0 & 0\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation $(A- {\\color{red}3} I){\\color{blue}\\mathbf{v}} = \\mathbf{0}$ corresponds to the following homogeneous system of linear equations:\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0 \\\\ 0=0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that $A-{\\color{red}3}I$ is already in row echelon form, and it has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. Moreover, from the first equation, we get $x_1=6x_2,$ which implies that the general solution is\n\n![](images/fa/fa0625bc99de3a27874b5695e72c9fd2e41ab618e49228086df7efcf7e1bb04f.svg)\n\nWe only require one eigenvector corresponding to $\\lambda={\\color{red}3}.$ Setting $x_2=1,$ we obtain the eigenvector\n\n![](images/bc/bcd87529387e7c400b7f5ccd896cfcbe3e42ab386a5b9d84b565f12752e2c4c3.svg) \n\n**Note:** If we set $x_2=2,$ we'll get a different eigenvector, namely\n![](images/83/83541fd42d19f0e3b17be1c36983d50d1382f36352168bce2d148126db7bf265.svg)\nNote that $\\mathbf w$ is also an eigenvector that corresponds to $\\lambda=3.$ In fact, we can choose any real $x_2 \\neq 0$ to generate an eigenvector corresponding to $\\lambda = 3.$ \n\n**Watch out!** In the case of $x_2=0,$ we get the zero vector, but this is not an eigenvector. Remember that eigenvectors must be non-zero vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "c585e113-f22f-5b5f-bfef-b3b81cd21acc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3562 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A$ with an eigenvalue $\\lambda$, the **eigenspace** $V_\\lambda$ can be defined as the set of all possible eigenvectors corresponding to $\\lambda$ plus the vector $\\mathbf{0}{:}$\n![](images/78/78c2c84d57ef00f32675c6d56fa91af39e0680eadf05ec266b0bdab9a57a8388.svg)\n\nNote that the eigenspace consists of *all* (not only non-zero) solutions of the equation $(A-\\lambda I)\\mathbf{x}=\\mathbf{0}.$ So, the eigenspace can also be viewed as the *null space* of the matrix $A-\\lambda I,$ as follows:\n\n$$\nV_{\\color{red}\\lambda} = \\textrm{Null}(A - {\\color{red}\\lambda} I).\n$$\n\nWe also have the following theorem:\n\n*Eigenvectors that correspond to different eigenvalues are always linearly independent.*\n\nFor example, the matrix 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
